draft.title: Testing for a right angle
card: If a triangle is right-angled, the square of its longest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides. The reverse is also true.
To test a triangle, find the longest side and square it. Then square the other two sides and add them. If the two results are equal, there is a right angle. If not, there is none.
Example: sides 7, 24 and 25. Longest side: \(25^{2} = 625\). Others: \(7^{2} + 24^{2} = 49 + 576 = 625\). They match, so the triangle is right-angled.
Three whole numbers that pass this test are called a Pythagorean triad. Two common ones are 3, 4, 5 and 5, 12, 13.
draft.remember: Square the longest side and compare it with the sum of the other two squares. Equal means a right angle.

a.q: A triangle has sides 9 cm, 12 cm and 15 cm. Which statement is correct?
a.why: \(9^{2} + 12^{2} = 81 + 144 = 225\), and \(15^{2} = 225\). The squares match, so there is a right angle. Adding the sides without squaring them does not test for a right angle.
a.clue: Square each side first, and start with the longest.

b.q: Priya cuts three timber pieces for a garden bed frame: 8 m, 15 m and 17 m. She wants a square corner. Which is the best conclusion?
b.why: The longest side is 17, and \(17^{2} = 289\). The others give \(64 + 225 = 289\), so the triangle has a right angle. The second option wrongly puts a shorter side on its own, when the longest side must be the one squared and compared.
b.clue: Which side is the longest? Square it first.

problems.detail: The right option stands out. It is the longest and the only one with a worked value (= 289 =), so a student could pick it without doing the test.
